paragraphs: Next to permanency in office, nothing can do more for the independence of the judges than a fixed provision for their support. The remark I made about the President applies equally here. In the general course of human nature, power over a man's subsistence amounts to power over his will. We can never hope to see the judicial power completely separated from the legislative in practice under any system that leaves the former dependent for its financial resources on the occasional grants of the latter. The enlightened friends of good government in every State have had reason to lament the lack of precise and explicit precautions on this point in the State constitutions. Some of them, it is true, have declared that permanent(1) salaries shall be established for the judges. But experience has shown, in some instances, that such expressions are not definite enough to prevent legislative evasions. Something still more positive and unequivocal has proved to be necessary. The plan of the Convention accordingly provides that the judges of the United States "shall at stated times receive for their services a compensation which shall not be diminished during their continuance in office."

All things considered, this is the best provision that could have been devised. It is easy to understand that fluctuations in the value of money and in the state of society made it inadmissible to fix a rate of compensation in the Constitution. What might be extravagant today might in half a century become meager and inadequate. It was therefore necessary to leave it to the discretion of the legislature to vary the provisions as circumstances vary, yet under such restrictions as to put it out of that body's power to make any individual's condition worse. A man may then be sure of the ground he stands on, and can never be deterred from his duty by fear of being placed in a less favorable situation. The clause I have quoted combines both advantages. The salaries of judicial officers may be altered from time to time as occasion requires, but never so as to reduce the allowance with which any particular judge comes into office, as far as he is concerned. It will be noticed that the Convention made a difference between the compensation of the President and that of the judges. The President's can be neither increased nor diminished; the judges' can only not be diminished. This probably arose from the difference in the length of the two offices. Since the President is to be elected for no more than four years, it can rarely happen that a salary adequate at the beginning of that period will fail to remain so to its end. But the judges, if they behave properly, will be secure in their places for life. It may well happen, especially in the early stages of the government, that a stipend quite sufficient when they are first appointed would become too small as their service goes on.

This provision for the judges' support shows every mark of prudence and effectiveness. We can say with confidence that, together with their permanent tenure, it gives them a better prospect of independence than the constitution of any State gives its own judges.

Their responsibility is secured by the article on impeachments. For misconduct they may be impeached by the House of Representatives and tried by the Senate; if convicted, they may be removed from office and barred from holding any other. This is the only provision on the point that is consistent with the necessary independence of the judicial character, and it is the only one in our own Constitution regarding our own judges.

Critics have complained that there is no provision for removing judges for inability. But all thoughtful men will recognize that such a provision would either go unused or be more open to abuse than able to serve any good end. Measuring the faculties of the mind has, I believe, no place among the known arts. An attempt to draw the line between ability and inability would far more often give room to personal and party attachments and enmities than serve justice or the public good. Except in cases of insanity, the result must mostly be arbitrary; and insanity, without any formal or express provision, may safely be pronounced a virtual disqualification.

The constitution of New York, to avoid investigations that must forever be vague and dangerous, has taken a particular age as the test of inability: no man can be a judge beyond sixty. I believe there are few at present who do not disapprove of this provision. There is no station for which it is less suitable than that of a judge. The deliberating and comparing faculties generally keep their strength well beyond that age in men who live past it. Consider this together with how few outlive the season of intellectual vigor, and how unlikely it is that any considerable part of the bench, whether larger or smaller, would be in that condition at the same time. We shall then be ready to conclude that limitations of this sort have little to recommend them. In a republic, where fortunes are not affluent and pensions not expedient, the dismissal of men from stations in which they have long and usefully served their country needs a better excuse to humanity than the imaginary danger of a superannuated bench. Such men depend on their posts for subsistence, and it will be too late for them to turn to any other occupation for a livelihood.
1. Vide Constitution of Massachusetts, Chapter 2, Section 1, Article 13.
